title: PostgreSQL Memory Hierarchy: Shared Buffers, OS Page Cache, and Double Buffering
realWorldScenario: A sysadmin allocates 60 GB of a 64 GB RAM server to PostgreSQL `shared_buffers`. Performance immediately degrades by 40%, and disk read latency spikes.
questionStatement: Explain the relationship between PostgreSQL `shared_buffers` and the Linux OS Kernel Page Cache. What is the "Double Buffering" architecture? Why is setting `shared_buffers` to 25% of RAM (16 GB on 64 GB) recommended, and how does `effective_cache_size` guide the query planner?
expectedConcepts: Buffered I/O via POSIX read/write and Linux Page Cache
Double buffering: page residing in both shared_buffers and kernel cache
Why 60GB shared_buffers starves OS page cache and causes swapping
effective_cache_size as an informational planner cost hint (not memory allocation)
hints: Does PostgreSQL use direct I/O (O_DIRECT) or buffered I/O by default?
Does setting effective_cache_size allocate physical RAM?
Why does PostgreSQL rely heavily on the Linux OS page cache?
